617.title: Make room
617.hook: when told to make room in assemblies, make room, and Allah makes room for you (58:11)
617.howItsDone: In mosques and gatherings, Muslims are taught to close up and make room for newcomers, especially in the rows of prayer and at the Friday sermon, and not to make anyone rise from their seat.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Mujadila, she who pleads her case, and your line, she was heard.

A crowded table at a family dinner. Someone arrives late, plate in hand, and stands there. Everyone is mid-conversation. Nobody moves. The latecomer hovers, then drifts to the kitchen counter to eat alone. It takes one person to say, here, squeeze in, and shift their chair six inches. Six inches, and someone belongs. Surah Al-Mujadila has a verse about that moment, set in the gatherings around the Prophet ﷺ in Medina, and it comes with a promise attached.

Verse eleven. Pickthall: "O ye who believe! when it is said, Make room! in assemblies, then make room; Allah will make way for you (hereafter)." The verb is tafassahu, make space, spread out, from the root f-s-h, wideness, roominess. Commentators report the setting: people sat close around the Prophet, and some latecomers, among them men who had fought at Badr, were left standing, because those seated didn't want to give up their places near him. The verse answers: make room. And notice the trade. You give up a few inches, and God makes room for you. Commentators read that widely: room in the grave, in paradise, in your life and your heart, in your provision. The verse continues: when you're told to rise, rise; God will raise those of you who believe, and those given knowledge, by degrees. Hadith fill in the manners. Bukhari and Muslim record that the Prophet said no one should make another person get up from his seat so that he can sit there. Instead, spread out and make room. So the rule cuts both ways. The one sitting should shift and make space. The one arriving shouldn't push anyone out. Between them, a crowded room gets bigger without a single chair added. In this verse, space isn't only something you have. It's something people make for each other.

Then think of one person standing at the edge of something, a new coworker, a quiet cousin, a neighbor, and picture moving your chair six inches for them.
Make room. When told to make room in gatherings, make room, and God will make room for you. Today's word.
Your line: squeeze in, shift six inches. The verse promises room in return. That's day six hundred seventeen.

618.title: Others before themselves
618.hook: the Ansar preferred others over themselves even in need (59:9)
618.howItsDone: Muslims tell the story of the Ansari couple and their guest as the model of ithar, and hospitality to guests, even when little is at hand, is a strongly emphasized virtue in Muslim communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday: make room, from Al-Mujadila, and your line, squeeze in, shift six inches. Today, Surah Al-Hashr, a step further.

A guest knocks at night. The family has one small meal in the house, just enough for the children. The husband and wife look at each other. They put the children to bed hungry, set the food before the guest, and the wife gets up, as if to fix the lamp, and puts it out. In the dark, the couple move their hands and mouths as if they're eating. The guest eats his fill. Nobody sees that nobody else ate. Except, the hadith says, someone did.

Bukhari and Muslim tell the story. A hungry man came to the Prophet ﷺ, who had nothing at home, and asked who would host him. A man of the Ansar, the Helpers of Medina, took him home; Muslim's report names him Abu Talha. In the morning, the Prophet told him God had marveled at what he and his wife had done for their guest. And the reports say this verse came down. Pickthall: they "prefer (the fugitives) above themselves though poverty become their lot." The fugitives are the Muhajirun, the emigrants who had fled Mecca with almost nothing. The Ansar had taken them in, shared homes, fields, even work. The verse praises them for three things: they love those who came to them, they feel no envy for what the newcomers were given, and they prefer them over themselves. That last is ithar, from the root '-th-r, to choose, to give preference. It's more than generosity. Generosity gives from extra. Ithar gives when there's no extra, when you'd go without. The verse ends: whoever is saved from the greed of his own soul, those are the successful. So the hardest part isn't the giving. It's the inner grip, the voice that says, but I need it too. Some writers on character call ithar the highest rank of generosity. The hadith gives it a picture: a darkened room, and a lamp put out on purpose, so a guest would think his hosts were eating too.

segments.voice: Think through your day, a parking spot, the last slice, the first turn to talk, credit for something done together, and find one place you could quietly let someone else have it. Notice the small grip inside that says, but I want it, and breathe into it.
Ithar. Preferring others over yourself, even when you're in need, as the Ansar did for the emigrants. Today's word.
Your line: others first. A lamp went out so a guest could eat. Day six hundred eighteen, done.

619.title: Look to tomorrow
619.hook: let every soul look at what it has sent ahead for tomorrow (59:18)
619.howItsDone: Muslims often recite 59:18 in Friday sermons as a call to self-reckoning, muhasaba, and many set up ongoing charities, sadaqa jariya, such as wells, schools or copies of the Qur'an, hoping their reward continues after death.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ithar, preferring others over yourself, like a lamp put out for a guest. Your line was others first.

Before a long trip, people send things ahead. A box shipped to the new address. A deposit on the apartment. A message to a friend at the other end: I land Thursday. When they arrive, what's waiting is exactly what they sent. Nothing more. Near its end, Surah Al-Hashr turns from the story of Medina to a single soul, and asks it to do what a careful traveler does the night before leaving: check what's already been sent on ahead.

Verse eighteen. Pickthall: "O ye who believe! Observe your duty to Allah. And let every soul look to that which it sendeth on before for the morrow." The word for tomorrow is ghad, the ordinary word for the day after today. Classical commentators read it here as the Day of Judgment. Why call it tomorrow? One answer they gave: it's so certain and so near, it's as close as tomorrow. The verb is qaddamat, what it has sent forward. Deeds are things you ship on before you. The command to be mindful of God, taqwa, comes twice, at the start and after the question, like bookends. The next verse warns: don't be like those who forgot God, so that God made them forget their own selves. Forgetting God and forgetting yourself are tied together. Hadith give the shipping list. Muslim records that the Prophet ﷺ said when a person dies, their deeds stop, except three: an ongoing charity, knowledge that benefits others, and a righteous child who prays for them. Three things that keep arriving after you've gone. And a report in Tirmidhi turns the accounting upside down. The family once slaughtered a sheep and gave nearly all of it away. 'A'isha told the Prophet only the shoulder was left. He answered: all of it is left, except its shoulder. What you keep is spent. What you send ahead stays.

segments.voice: Picture yourself a year from now, looking back on today: what would that person thank you for? A kindness that outlasts the day, a small amount given, something learned and passed on, a call to a parent. Choose one, and ask quietly: what have I sent ahead?

620.title: A mountain humbled
620.hook: had We sent this Qur'an on a mountain, you'd see it humbled and split (59:21)
620.howItsDone: The last verses of Surah Al-Hashr, from this verse to the end, are often recited together, and many Muslims read 59:21 as a call to let the Qur'an soften the heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ghad, tomorrow, and the deeds a soul sends on ahead. Your line was what have I sent ahead?

A mountain doesn't move. Lean your whole weight on one and it won't notice. It was there before everyone you know was born, and it'll be there after. Weather breaks on it. Centuries go past it. It's hard to imagine anything that could make a mountain tremble. Surah Al-Hashr, in its closing verses, imagines exactly that. And what shakes the mountain isn't an earthquake. It's a book.

Verse twenty-one. Pickthall: "If We had caused this Qur'an to descend upon a mountain, thou (O Muhammad) verily hadst seen it humbled, rent asunder by the fear of Allah." Two words carry the picture. Khashi'an, humbled, from the same root as khushu', the stillness of prayer we met a week ago. And mutasaddi'an, split, cracking apart. The mountain bows, then breaks. Then the verse explains itself: such parables we strike for people, so that they may reflect. The point lands on us. If this speech would humble a mountain, what is it doing to a human heart that hears it and stays the same? The Qur'an has shown a mountain like this before. In Surah Al-A'raf, Musa asks to see God. He's told to look at the mountain: if it stays in place, you will see me. When his Lord revealed himself to the mountain, it crumbled to dust, and Musa fell down senseless. And in Surah Al-Ahzab, God offers the trust to the heavens, the earth and the mountains. They decline it, afraid of it, and the human being takes it on. The mountains in the Qur'an know their limits. Here's the startling reversal: the hardest thing in the landscape trembles, while a person can hear the same words and feel nothing. The verse doesn't scold. It holds up the mountain like a mirror and leaves its hearers to reflect.
screen: `KHASHI'AN: HUMBLED.` · `MUTASADDI'AN: SPLIT APART.` · `MUSA AND THE MOUNTAIN.` · `A MIRROR: SO THAT THEY MAY REFLECT.`

segments.voice: If you can see a hill, a tall building or even a big tree, stand and face it; if not, close your eyes and picture the largest mountain you've ever seen. Stand tall, feet planted, and feel how solid you are, and how solid it is. If you pray, let your shoulders soften a little in humility before what's greater; if not, simply notice what it's like to be small next to something vast.

621.title: The names at the end
621.hook: He is Allah, the King, the Holy, Peace, the Faithful … the Creator, the Fashioner (59:22–24)
621.howItsDone: Many Muslims recite the last three verses of Surah Al-Hashr, especially morning and evening, and learn the names of God, often from the list of ninety-nine, as a form of remembrance.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Musa, and the mountain that would crumble under the Qur'an. Your line was the mountain would crumble.

Anyone who has written a birthday card for their mother knows the problem. One word won't do. Kind, but also stubborn. Funny, and also the one who stayed up when you were sick. Every word catches one side and misses the rest, so the card turns into a list. Surah Al-Hashr ends with a list too. Three verses, each beginning He is Allah, then names, one after another, eleven of them in the last two verses alone.
screen: `HE IS ALLAH, HE IS ALLAH, HE IS ALLAH.`

segments.voice: Verse twenty-two: he is God, other than whom there is no god, the knower of the unseen and the seen, the Merciful, the Compassionate. Verse twenty-three, in Pickthall: "He is Allah, than Whom there is no other God, the Sovereign Lord, the Holy One, Peace, the Keeper of Faith, the Guardian, the Majestic, the Compeller, the Superb." In Arabic: al-Malik, al-Quddus, as-Salam, al-Mu'min, al-Muhaymin, al-'Aziz, al-Jabbar, al-Mutakabbir. Eight names in one breath. Then verse twenty-four: "He is Allah, the Creator, the Shaper out of naught, the Fashioner. His are the most beautiful names." Al-Khaliq, al-Bari', al-Musawwir. Commentators read these three as stages of making: al-Khaliq determines and plans, al-Bari' brings into being, al-Musawwir gives each thing its form. Planner, maker, shaper. Then the phrase for the whole idea: lahul-asma'ul-husna, his are the most beautiful names. And the surah ends where it began: everything in the heavens and the earth glorifies him. A hadith in Bukhari and Muslim says God has ninety-nine names, and whoever learns and keeps them enters paradise. The familiar list of ninety-nine comes from a report in Tirmidhi, and many scholars think narrators gathered that list rather than the Prophet ﷺ speaking it himself. But the names in these three verses are straight from the Qur'an, and many Muslims know them by heart. No single name says it all. That's why there are so many.
screen: `THE KNOWER OF THE UNSEEN AND SEEN.` · `EIGHT NAMES IN ONE BREATH.` · `PLANNER, MAKER, SHAPER.` · `HIS ARE THE MOST BEAUTIFUL NAMES.`

If that isn't yours, take three of the English words, Peace, the Holy, the Fashioner, and let one sit on each out-breath. Notice which one stays with you.
Al-Hashr, the surah that closes with name after name for God: eight in one breath, then planner, maker, shaper, and the most beautiful names. Today's word.
Your line: his are the beautiful names. One word was never going to be enough. That's day six hundred twenty-one.

622.title: Ibrahim, an example
622.hook: in Ibrahim and those with him is an excellent example (60:4)
622.tomorrow: Kindness to those who don't fight you
622.howItsDone: Muslims honor Ibrahim as the friend of God, khalil Allah, and invoke him in every prayer; his hospitality is held up as a model, and Muslim hosts often speak of honoring the guest as a duty of faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the end of Surah Al-Hashr, name after name for God. Your line was his are the beautiful names. Today, Surah sixty, She who is Tested.

An excellent example. In Surah Al-Ahzab, the Qur'an uses that phrase for the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. In Surah sixty it uses it again, this time for Ibrahim, Abraham, the friend of God, and those who stood beside him. Being named an example is a heavy honor. People are meant to copy you, and copying is never abstract: it's how you speak, who you stand up to, who you feed. Surah sixty shows two sides of Ibrahim at once, and quietly marks one thing not to copy.

Verse four. Pickthall: "There is a goodly pattern for you in Abraham and those with him". The Arabic is uswa hasana, an excellent example, the same phrase Al-Ahzab uses for the Prophet. Then the verse says what the pattern is. Ibrahim and those with him told their own people, plainly, that they would not worship what their people worshipped besides God. They stood firm, even against their own families. That's one side. The surah, named for a woman who is tested, was revealed at a time of divided loyalties, and it speaks to people torn between faith and family. But the same verse makes one exception: Ibrahim's words to his father, I will ask forgiveness for you, though I have no power to do anything for you against God. The verse sets that promise outside the pattern, and Surah At-Tawbah says Ibrahim later stopped asking forgiveness for his father, once it was clear his father was an enemy to God. Still, the way he spoke is remembered. Surah Maryam keeps the moment: Ibrahim says to his father, peace be upon you, I will ask my Lord to forgive you. Firm in belief, gentle in speech. That's the second side. And elsewhere the Qur'an shows a third: his table. In Surah Adh-Dhariyat, strangers arrive at Ibrahim's door. He doesn't know who they are. He hurries to his family and comes back with a fattened calf. Firm, tender, and quick to feed a stranger. The verse calls the whole pattern beautiful.
screen: `USWA HASANA: AN EXCELLENT EXAMPLE.` · `FIRM WITH HIS PEOPLE.` · `TENDER WITH HIS FATHER.` · `A FATTENED CALF FOR STRANGERS.`

Ibrahim. In him and those with him, Surah sixty says, is an excellent example: firm in faith, tender with his father, generous at his table. Today's word.

623.title: Kindness to those who don't fight you
623.hook: Allah doesn't forbid kindness and justice toward those who haven't fought you (60:8)
623.tomorrow: Why say what you don't do?
623.howItsDone: Muslim scholars cite 60:8 in teaching good relations with neighbors of other faiths, and the story of Asma' bint Abi Bakr and her mother is often told to show that family ties continue across differences of belief.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ibrahim, firm in faith, tender with his father, quick to feed strangers. Your line was an excellent example. Today closes the week.

Asma', the daughter of Abu Bakr, is living in Medina when her mother arrives from Mecca. The mother hasn't become Muslim. Mecca is the city that drove the daughter's community out. One report says the mother came bearing gifts. Asma' doesn't know what to do. Should she let her in? Accept the gifts? Can she be kind to her own mother across this line? She goes to ask the Prophet ﷺ.
screen: `CAN SHE BE KIND ACROSS THE LINE?`

segments.voice: Bukhari and Muslim record his answer. Yes, he said: keep good ties with your mother. Some reports connect this verse to her story. Surah sixty, verse eight. Pickthall: "Allah forbiddeth you not those who warred not against you on account of religion and drove you not out from your homes, that ye should show them kindness and deal justly with them. Lo! Allah loveth the just dealers." Two words do the work. The first is tabarruhum, show them kindness, from the root b-r-r, the same root as birr, the word the Qur'an and hadith use for kindness to parents. The second is tuqsitu, deal justly, from qist, fairness. And the verse ends with God's love for the muqsitin, the people of fairness. So this isn't permission for a cold politeness. It uses family words. People of another faith who live in peace with the community may be shown birr and qist: warmth and fairness. The surah came in a hard time, when the community was in conflict with Mecca, and the next verse draws a line around those who actually fought them and drove them out. Scholars have discussed how the two verses fit together across history. But the core of verse eight is plain: kindness and fairness are not forbidden, and fairness is loved. A mother at the door, not a Muslim. The answer: yes, be good to her.
screen: `ASMA' AND HER MOTHER.` · `TABARRUHUM: SHOW THEM BIRR.` · `QIST: DEAL JUSTLY.` · `GOD LOVES THE PEOPLE OF FAIRNESS.`

segments.voice: Think of someone whose faith, or lack of one, is different from yours: a neighbor, a coworker, a relative, a friend. Picture their face, and breathe in warmth toward them, breathe out fairness. Then choose one small, concrete kindness, a message, a favor, a genuine question about their week, and hold it until it feels doable.
Birr: kindness, the root behind God's permission in Surah Al-Mumtahanah to be warm and fair with those who haven't fought you over faith. Today's word.
Your line: kindness and justice to all. The week ran from deeds sent ahead, through the humbled mountain and the beautiful names, to Ibrahim and Asma' at her door. A full week, done.
